title: Twitter Timeline & Search
blurb: Fan-out on write, celebrity merge at read time, caching and search
summary: Users post tweets, read a home timeline built from everyone they follow, and search. Reads dwarf writes, so the home timeline is precomputed: each new tweet is pushed into followers' timelines in memory (fan-out on write), except for celebrities, whose tweets are merged in when a timeline is read.

nodes.label: Web Server
nodes.subtitle: A reverse proxy in front of…

nodes.label: Memory Cache (Redis)
nodes.subtitle: Each home timeline is a list…

steps.title: Client → Web Server
steps.text: @devnews posts a tweet. The Client sends it to the Web Server (a reverse proxy), which forwards it to the Write API.

steps.title: Write API → SQL Database
steps.text: The Write API saves the tweet to the author's own timeline in the SQL Database. That is the user timeline: the author's own tweets, in order.
steps.data:
INSERT INTO tweets (tweet_id, user_id, text, created_at)
VALUES (1849302284, 204, 'hello world!', now());

steps.title: Object Store
steps.text: Media goes to the Object Store, not the database: a tweet row stays small, and photos and videos are served from cheap blob storage (usually behind a CDN).
steps.data: PUT s3://tweet-media/ABC987.jpg  (≈ 10 KB average per tweet incl. media)

steps.title: Write API → Fan Out Service
steps.text: The Write API hands the tweet to the Fan Out Service, which asks the User Graph Service who follows the author. The follower lists live in the Memory Cache.

steps.title: Fan-out on write
steps.text: Fan-out on write: the tweet id is pushed onto the home timeline of each of the 12,000 followers in the Memory Cache. It is O(n): 12,000 followers means 12,000 inserts, and each list is trimmed to its newest 800.
steps.data:
# for each follower f (pipelined, batched)
LPUSH home:<f> "1849302284:204:0"
LTRIM home:<f> 0 799

→ 12,000 list writes

steps.title: Fan Out Service → Search Cluster
steps.text: The tweet is added to the Search Cluster so keyword searches can find it within seconds.

steps.title: Fan Out Service → Notification Service
steps.text: Notifications go out through the Notification Service, which works off a queue so a slow push or email provider never delays the post.

steps.title: Write API → Client
steps.text: The author gets a response as soon as the tweet is saved; fan-out, indexing and notifications carry on in the background.

takeaways: The home timeline is read far more than tweets are written, so build it ahead of time: fan out on write.
Fan-out is O(followers): fine for most users, far too slow for celebrities.
Skip fan-out for accounts with millions of followers and merge their tweets in at read time.
Keep timelines in memory, only the newest few hundred tweets, and only for active users.
credit: Adapted from Design the Twitter timeline and search, Donne Martin, System Design Primer (CC BY 4.0)
